Before you buy python leather

Know the snake behind the skin

Six python species supply most of the world’s python leather, and their close relatives can be passed off as them. Each has its own colours, its own IUCN Red List status and its own CITES rules. Explore them by genus, compare any two, test your eye, then ask the right question in the shop. (VKM, 2023)

Species guide

Which python could your leather come from?

Eleven species from the family Pythonidae, grouped by genus. Each card shows a real photo of that species. Real skins vary, and tanned or dyed leather can hide the pattern completely, so a pattern is a clue, never proof.

Side by side

From buyer to protector

Turn the bag over: which snake is inside?

Every python bag, wallet or shoe was once a living snake. Tap each item to see which python it could come from, how at risk that species is, and the one move that turns a buyer into a protector.

Real python goods

What luxury brands have done. Chanel stopped using exotic skins, including python, in 2018 (Fortune, 2018). Kering, owner of Gucci, helped found the Python Conservation Partnership to study a sustainable trade (ITC; IUCN, 2016). We show no brand products or logos here: ask any brand the same three questions.
Test your eye

Skin quiz: which python is this?

Look at the pattern and colours, then pick a species. Each answer tells you its Red List status. Notice how alike some skins look: that is why a label needs proof behind it.

Solution 2 · R keyword monitor

Find python-skin listings that show no proof

Our R Shiny app, rebuilt to run here in the browser with the same keywords and scoring. Search the listings, or click each step to see what the tool does. A flag is not proof that a listing is illegal: a person always decides. Method follows Di Minin et al. (2019) and Xu et al. (2019).

IUCN Red List

Where each species sits

The Red List measures extinction risk. A species can be legal to trade and still be at risk.

LCLeast Concern
NTNear Threatened
VUVulnerable
ENEndangered
CRCritically Endangered

Sources: IUCN Red List assessments for each species (2012–2021); see the species cards for the year of each assessment.

Reading the label

What “wild” and “captive-bred” really mean

Every CITES permit carries a source code. Buyers almost never see it, but sellers can ask their supplier for it. (CITES Res. Conf. 12.3)

W
Taken from the wild

Legal when it comes from a set quota, such as Indonesia’s 175,000 pythons a year with a 240 cm minimum size (CITES, 2022; Shine et al., 1999).

C
Bred in captivity

Born to parents bred in captivity. Research has found wild snakes passed through farms with this label (Lyons & Natusch, 2011).

F
Born in captivity

Born on a farm to a wild-caught mother. Ask how many breeding adults the farm keeps.

R
Ranched

Raised in captivity from eggs or young collected in the wild.

?
“Sustainable” tag only

A brand claim with no permit, tag or audit behind it. Treat it as weak proof.

Proof meter

What did the seller show you?

One question
“Can you show me the source?”

Three things to ask for

  1. Which source code is on the permit (W, C, F or R)?
  2. Is there a tag or traceability ID linked to species and country?
  3. Who verified it, and how?

No answer? Choose a verified item, or wait. Asking is the signal that changes what shops stock.

Why this guide

What this site does that others don’t

The IUCN Red List, CITES Species+ and brand pages each hold part of the answer. This guide joins them up for a shopper.

  • All skin-trade pythons on one pageEleven species, grouped by genus, side by side. The Red List and Species+ show one species per page.
  • Status, rules and year togetherEvery card shows the IUCN category, its assessment year and the CITES Appendix.
  • Real photos of every skinA real photo of each species’ skin pattern, so you can compare what the leather would look like.
  • Interactive, not a wall of textClick the family tree, filter, search, compare any two species and test yourself in the skin quiz.
  • Tells you what to askThree questions and a proof meter turn knowledge into one action at the till.
  • Plain words, two languagesEnglish and 中文, readable in 30 seconds on a phone. Free, no login, no ads.
  • Every fact has a sourceIUCN assessments, CITES documents and peer-reviewed studies are listed below.
